youtube.title: C++ Linked List from Scratch | C++ Programming EP 85
youtube.description: In this episode you will build a linked list with nodes, walk along a list and free every node, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Linked list · 1:19 Build, walk and free · 2:55 Three nodes on the heap · 3:35 Second program · 5:01 Recap · 5:32 Bug of the Day · 6:25 Challenge · 6:50 Next episode

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we build our first data structure. A linked list is a chain of nodes, and each node points to the next one.

scenes.onScreen: "Linked list": numbered lines (1. A node holds a value and a pointer; 2. The head points to the first node; 3. Free every node when you finish) and an analogy card: train cars: each car knows only the next car
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: A node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. The last node points to null. A pointer called head points to the first node. Think of train cars. Each car knows only the next car. To reach the last car, you walk along the train. Why learn a linked list when we have a vector? The list teaches you how data structures are built from nodes and pointers. Every tree and graph uses the same idea. A vector keeps its items side by side. A list keeps them anywhere, and the pointers join them. Adding to the front of a list is quick, because nothing else moves.
points: A node holds a value and a pointer
The head points to the first node
Free every node when you finish

scenes.onScreen: list.cpp: three nodes are linked, printed, and freed
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 4] A node has a value and a pointer to the next node. [HL 10] New makes the first node on the heap. The head pointer keeps its address. [HL 11] The next pointer of the first node points to a second node. [HL 12] The same step adds a third node. [HL 13] The walker cur starts at the head. [HL 13] Each step moves cur to the next node. The loop stops at null. The output is ten twenty thirty. [HL 18] To free the list, first save the next pointer. [HL 19] Then delete the node. [HL 20] Then move on. If you delete first, you lose the way forward. [HL 4] A node holds a value and a pointer to the next node. [HL 10] The first node holds ten, and head points at it. [HL 11] The second node is added through the next pointer of the first. [HL 13] The loop starts at head, and follows the next pointers. It stops at null. [HL 17] At the end, we free the nodes one by one. We save the next pointer first, or we would lose the rest of the list.

scenes.onScreen: memory boxes: head and three nodes joined by next pointers
scenes.animation: Boxes pop in one by one with size and address tags; arrows draw on as the narrator mentions them; regions are labelled; pop per box
scenes.narration: The head pointer lives on the stack. The three nodes live on the heap. Each next pointer holds the address of the next node. The last pointer is null, so the walk stops there. Notice that the nodes can sit far apart in memory. Only the arrows connect them. If you lose the head, you lose the whole list. So never overwrite head before you save it.

scenes.onScreen: push.cpp: a function adds a node at the front of the list
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 9] This function makes a new node, and its next pointer is the old head. The new node is now the first one. [HL 29] An empty list has a null head. [HL 31] Each call returns the new head, so we store it. [HL 33] We add one, then two, then three, each at the front. The list prints three two one. [HL 34] Free list deletes every node. [HL 9] This function makes a new node, and its next pointer is the old head. The new node becomes the new head. [HL 31] Pushing one, two and three gives the list three, two, one. [HL 33] The print function walks the list. [HL 34] The free function releases every node.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as push dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints ten twenty thirty, and then three two one. Notice the order. The last number pushed is the first one printed.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. A node holds a value and a next pointer. Two. The head points to the first node. Three. Walk the list until the pointer is null. Four. Save the next pointer before you delete a node. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: A node holds a value and a next pointer.
The head points to the first node.
Walk the list until the pointer is null.
Save the next pointer before you delete a node.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: The walk stops one node early
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The list holds one, two and three, but the output shows only one and two. The loop tests the next pointer. It stops on the last node, before it prints. Test cur itself. Think about what the loop test means. When cur is the last node, its next pointer is null. If the test looks at next, the loop stops one node too early. Test cur itself, and the last node is included.

scenes.onScreen: Why did the node feel lonely? It only ever knew the next one.
scenes.animation: Full tomato screen, card flips in with a rimshot, Xecxec snaps his claw
scenes.narration: Why did the node feel lonely? It only ever knew the next one.

scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a function that counts the nodes in a linked list. An empty list has zero nodes. Hint: start the count at zero, walk the list, and add one for each node. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.animation: Next-episode card slides up with a whoosh; right side stays empty for end-screen elements; sign-off text types in
scenes.narration: Next time: binary tree. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Program output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

1 2
bug.why: The test cur next not null stops at the last node, before it prints. Test cur itself. It is null only after the last node.

pun: "Why did the node feel lonely? It only ever knew the next one."
challenge: Write a function that counts the nodes in a linked list. An empty list has zero nodes. Hint: start the count at zero, walk the list, and add one for each node.
challengeAnswer: Set a counter to zero. Walk with a pointer from the head until null. Add one on each step.
